## The Workaround Economy


The workaround economy is every spreadsheet, copy-paste step, side inbox and unanswered feature request that a business uses to cover the gap between its tools and its work. Each workaround looks small. Together they become the real operating system of the business, and nobody owns it, tests it or improves it.


Most businesses do not run on their software. They run on the space between their software. A sales lead arrives in a form tool, gets copied into a spreadsheet, gets pasted into a CRM, and gets a follow-up email that someone writes by hand. A client asks for a status update, and an account manager searches three places to answer. A machine needs service, and the reminder lives in one person's calendar.


None of these steps is a failure of effort. They are a failure of fit. The software was built for the average customer of the vendor, and your business is not the average customer. So the people closest to the work fill the gap with what they have. Retool's 2020 State of Internal Tools survey found that Google Sheets was the most popular software for building internal tools. The spreadsheet is the oldest app builder in the office.


Workaround Where it lives What it costs the business


A shadow spreadsheet A shared drive, one tab per person Two versions of the truth, and nobody knows which one is current


Copy and paste between tools Browser tabs and clipboards Hours of manual entry, and errors that nobody sees until a customer does


A side inbox for requests Email folders and chat threads Requests that wait, get lost or get answered twice


A feature request to the vendor The vendor's roadmap A wait with no date, for a change that may never fit your process


A ticket to the internal team The engineering queue Business problems compete with product work, and they usually lose


A reminder in one person's head Memory and calendars The process stops when that person is on vacation


The cost of the workaround economy is rarely on an invoice. It shows up as slow answers, missed follow-ups, and the quiet decision to stop asking for improvements. A team that stops asking stops improving.


The backlog is the visible part of this economy. In agile teams, a backlog is a ranked list of work for a product team (see the[wiki entry on the backlog](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/scrum/backlog) ). In most small and mid-size businesses, the software backlog is less formal. It is a set of complaints about the tools that people stopped saying out loud.

## Who Changes the Tool When the Work Changes?


The people closest to the work are the operations leads, account managers, coordinators and owners who see each problem first. They know which field is missing, which step repeats and which customer question comes back every week. Until now, they could describe the fix but could not build it. AI app builders change who can build.


The dispatcher who moves jobs every morning knows what a field-service schedule needs. The account manager who answers the same three questions every Friday knows what a client portal must show. In the old model, their knowledge passed through a chain: a request, a meeting, a spec, a ticket, a sprint, a release. Each step lost detail and added time.

Who builds the change? A vendor or a developer The person doing the work, with Taskade Genesis and Taskade EVE

The table has one honest limit. Removing handoffs removes delay, but it also removes review. A developer who ships a change also asks, "What breaks if I do this?" When an operator builds, that question still needs an owner. Most of this essay is about how to keep that question alive without bringing back the queue. ## Feedback-to-Fix Latency Across Five Eras


Feedback-to-fix latency is the time from the first report of a real operational problem to a verified change that people use. For fifty years, that latency depended on someone else: the IT department, the ERP consultant, the SaaS vendor. AI-built software is the first era in which the person who reports the problem can also make the change.


The table below asks one maintenance question of each era: when a tool must change, where does the request wait, and what sets the latency? It gives no wait-time numbers, because no reliable source measures them across eras. For the dated history of build vs buy, read[When Customers Build Their Own Software](https://www.taskade.com/blog/build-vs-buy-software) .


Era Where the change request waits What people do while it waits What sets the feedback-to-fix latency


Mainframe IT The IT queue Paper forms and manual steps The priorities of the IT department


Packaged ERP A release cycle or a change project A spreadsheet beside the system The release calendar and the consultant budget


SaaS The vendor roadmap Feature requests and workarounds What the vendor builds for its average customer


Low-code A builder license and an IT review Shadow tools How fast IT reviews each new tool


AI-built software A prompt, then a verification step They make the change and check it How fast the owner verifies the change with real records


Each era moved the change one step closer to the work, and each left a workaround behind: the paper form, the spreadsheet beside the ERP, the shadow tool beside the SaaS app. In 2025, the workaround and the fix can be the same thing. The person who would have built a spreadsheet can now build the tool, if they also learn to verify it.

## The New Software Factory


Guillermo Rauch, CEO of Vercel, describes a business as a software factory that turns signals into fixes, and he says the measure is the latency from signal to shipped fix. In an October 2026 interview, he separated iteration speed from iteration velocity and argued for verification, not micro unit tests, as the guardrail. For the definition, the history and the metrics of the category, see our guide to the[AI software factory](https://www.taskade.com/blog/ai-software-factory) .


Rauch gave the[interview](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WeiB_gLOdQE) on the David Ondrej channel on October 2, 2026. His examples come from a software company, but four of his ideas apply to any business that builds its own tools.


**1. A rubric for how agentic a company is.** Rauch proposed three questions. When a customer reaches out, do you reply with a high-quality response? When they report a problem, do you start an investigation? When they report a concrete, fixable thing, do you fix it? Then measure the latency from signal to shipped fix. At one end, a company reviews feedback now and then. At the other end, it becomes autonomous "in a good way", which does not mean agents that run wild.


He also kept a place for judgment. Some feedback is objective, such as an exception in production or a clear improvement. Other feedback, such as "the navigation confuses me", is good but not something you can turn into a prompt. A person still decides.


**2. Speed is not velocity.** Vercel separates iteration speed, how fast you turn out work, from iteration velocity, speed in a direction. Rauch warned that you can land changes "into oblivion". His advice was to pick a few problems where you have an advantage and go deep on them.


**3. Verification engineering.** Rauch describes verification engineering as the work of setting guardrails, a "proof system", around what you build. You and the agent agree on the axioms and the trade-offs. He is skeptical of micro unit tests that give false confidence. He would rather spend effort on the edges of the system: what must be correct, what it must feel like, and what you will not trade off.


**4. Know your customer.** Building is easy when you are the customer, because the test is whether you like the app. Selling to others is different. Rauch likes a metric called **error-free sessions** : one real visitor, start to finish, with every step working.

The third row needs an honest note. Taskade does not ship a fix to your app on its own when a signal arrives. A person still asks for the change, and a person still checks it. ## What Happens After the Weekend?


After the weekend, an app meets real customers, changing requirements, growing data, new people who need access, and steps that must run without anyone watching. A weekend build answers "can it work?" Month six answers "does it still work?" The second answer depends on data, permissions, automations and verification, not on the first prompt.


The phrase "in a weekend" in the Garry Tan post is true. A first version in a weekend is now normal. But a business does not run on first versions. Garry Tan named the risk himself in March 2025, when TechCrunch reported on the YC W25 batch. He pictured a startup with 95% AI-generated code and 100 million users a year or two later, and asked: "Does it fall over or not?"


Here is what changes when real use begins.


**Real customers.** The first customer finds the case you did not think about, such as a phone number in the name field. You learn about it from a person, not a test.


**Changing requirements.** A new service line needs a new field, and a new rule needs an approval step. A tool you can change in chat keeps up. A tool you must request changes from falls behind again.


**Persistent data.** A demo can lose its data. A CRM cannot. In Taskade, the data lives in workspace projects, outside any one app, so you can rebuild a screen without losing a record.


**Permissions.** More people need access, and not all of them need the same access. Workspace members get role-based access from Owner to Viewer. App visitors are different. Client sign-in works on every plan. Sign-in tells the app who the visitor is. It does not hide other people's records on its own. You match records to the login, and you test it with a second account. See[App Users](https://www.taskade.com/learn/genesis/app-users) .


**Automation.** The reminder, the follow-up and the weekly summary must run when nobody is looking. An app without automations is a screen. An app with automations is a process.


**Verification.** Every change must be checked against the outcome. Taskade Genesis keeps saved app revisions that you can preview and restore, and it can detect app errors and attempt a targeted repair. See[App Revisions & Restore](https://www.taskade.com/learn/genesis/version-history) and[AI error recovery](https://www.taskade.com/learn/genesis/error-fixing) .

Rauch's warning about slop applies here too. If anyone can one-shot an app, a one-shot app adds no value. The value comes from what you add after the first version: your data, your rules, your follow-up steps and your checks.

## Vibe Coded App Maintenance: What Breaks in Month Two?


Vibe coded app maintenance is the work of keeping an AI-built app correct after real people use it. In month two, the usual failures are sign-in problems, triggers that stop, expired integration keys, used-up credits, growing data, outdated packages and edits that break another page. Most of them are quiet, so someone must look for them.


In month one, nothing has changed and the builder remembers every detail. In month two, the business changes, edge cases arrive and the builder forgets why a field exists. Two public studies show why code-level maintenance is hard.


- **Security.** Veracode's 2025 GenAI Code Security Report found that AI-generated code introduced security flaws in 45% of tests, across 80 coding tasks and more than 100 models. The figure is per task, not per app, but every task is a place to look.
- **Code quality drift.** GitClear's AI Copilot Code Quality 2025 research found that copy-pasted lines rose from 8.3% to 12.3% of changed lines from 2021 to 2024, while moved (refactored) lines fell to under 10%. More copied code means more places to fix the same bug.


Both studies describe code that someone maintains in a repository. A hosted workspace removes part of that work, but not the part about your data, your rules and your access. The ledger below lists the common failures and where the fix lives in each world.

The pattern in the ledger is simple. In a repository, most fixes need a developer and a deploy. In a workspace, most fixes need an owner and a check. That is why the owner matters more than the builder.

## A Maintenance Cadence You Can Copy


A maintenance cadence is a fixed schedule of small checks that keeps an AI-built app correct: one check for each change, a short daily scan, a weekly review of open requests and a monthly review of access, cost and latency. The cadence below fits a small team and needs no developer.


Most app failures are not dramatic. A trigger stops, a key expires, a field changes meaning. A cadence turns those quiet failures into scheduled checks. Copy the table into a Taskade project and assign each row to a person.

Each change The change works with real data Submit a real record, open the app as a second account, check the automation run The record, the screen and the run all agree


Each change You can go back Note the current app revision before you publish You know which revision to restore


Daily New requests and failed steps Scan the requests project and the automation run history Every new request has an owner


Weekly Open requests Review the open list, close what is verified The list is shorter or each item has a date

The last step feeds the first one. What you see while you watch becomes the next report. Here is the same cadence as a checklist you can paste into a project:


- Before each change, note the live app revision.
- After each change, test with one real record.
- After each change, open the app as a second account.
- After each change, confirm the automation run in the run history.

- Each week, close the requests you verified.
- Each week, ask the agent three real questions and compare the answers with the records.
- Each month, review members, App Users and credit use.
- Each month, write down your feedback-to-fix latency.

## What Not to Maintain Yourself


Some systems carry a maintenance burden that a specialist vendor carries better: payments, payroll and tax, regulated records and security tools for your staff. Their rules change by country and by year, and each one adds what Rauch calls **security debt** : more attack surface to defend. Buy these, and let the vendor keep them current.


Maintain the layer around them that changes with your process: CRM views, client portals, intake forms and dashboards. Automations connect the two, because triggers pull events in from the system you bought and actions push data out to it.

## The Workspace Is the Foundation


A business tool keeps running when it sits on a workspace where projects remember, agents reason, automations run and apps serve. Taskade calls this Workspace DNA: Memory, Intelligence and Execution. An app that sits alone on a server is a screen. An app on a workspace is a process the team can change.


The screen is what you see in a demo, but it is the smallest part of a business tool. The rest is the data, the reasoning and the repeat steps. If those live somewhere else, every change to the screen is a new integration project.


Workspace DNA layer Taskade part Its job in a business tool

Intelligence AI agents Read the records, answer questions, triage requests, draft replies


Execution Automations Run reminders, follow-ups, approvals and syncs with 100+ integrations


Interface Taskade Genesis apps Serve the right view to staff, clients and partners


The loop is what makes the workspace a foundation. Memory feeds Intelligence. Intelligence triggers Execution. Execution creates new Memory. A form entry becomes a record. An agent reads the record and flags it. An automation sends the follow-up and logs it. The log becomes context for the next request. Each change starts from more context than the last one.


This is the argument of[Software That Runs Itself](https://www.taskade.com/blog/software-runs-itself) and[Agentic Workspaces](https://www.taskade.com/blog/agentic-workspaces) , applied to the backlog. The workspace is what makes the second change cheap. Without it, every change is a rebuild. With it, a change is a sentence.

## The Next Competitive Advantage


The next competitive advantage is not who has the most software. It is how fast a business turns a real operational problem into a working, verified change. Feedback-to-fix latency and iteration velocity are the numbers to watch. Every business can build now, so the edge goes to the one that fixes faster and checks its fixes.


When every business can build, building stops being the edge. The edge moves to the loop: how fast a signal reaches the person who can act, how fast that person can change the tool, and how sure they are that the change works. Here is a simple scorecard to start with.


Metric What to count Where to track it


Feedback-to-fix latency Time from the first report to a verified change A project with one record per request, with a reported date and a verified date


Iteration velocity Problems solved and verified per month The same project, filtered by status


Error-free sessions Visitors who finish a task with no failed step Your own checks, with real records


Workarounds retired Spreadsheets and manual steps you removed A short list that the team reviews each month


Open requests Problems reported but not fixed The same project, as the backlog you can see


Start small. Pick one workaround that annoys your team every week. Describe the job in Taskade Genesis, or clone a kit on a paid plan. Make one change, verify it with real data, and write down how long it took from the first complaint to the verified change. That number is your feedback-to-fix latency. Next month, make it smaller.

## Frequently Asked Questions


What is the software backlog?


The software backlog is the list of changes a business needs from its tools but cannot get on its own schedule. It holds feature requests sent to vendors, tickets waiting for an internal developer, and the spreadsheets and manual steps that people use in the meantime. When the person closest to the work can build and change the tool, that list gets shorter.


What is feedback-to-fix latency?


Feedback-to-fix latency is the time from the first report of a real operational problem to a verified change that people use. A report can be a customer email, a form entry, a comment or a failed step. The clock stops only when the change is live and someone has checked that it works with real data.


Can a nontechnical person build business software in a weekend?


A nontechnical person can build a working first version in a weekend. Taskade Genesis builds a live app with its database from one prompt, and Taskade EVE edits it in chat. The weekend is the start. Real customers, changing requirements, permissions and automations decide whether the app keeps working on Monday and in month six.


What happens to an AI-built app after the first version?


After the first version, the app meets real use. Records pile up, requirements change, new people need access and the business asks for new steps. In Taskade, the data stays in workspace projects, agents work with that data, automations run the repeat steps, and Taskade Genesis keeps saved app revisions that you can preview and restore.


Who fixes a vibe coded app when it breaks?


The person who owns the app fixes it, so name that owner before launch. When the app lives in a code repository, a developer usually reads logs, changes code and redeploys. In a Taskade workspace, the owner can ask Taskade EVE for the fix in chat, use AI error recovery, or restore an earlier app revision.


Can I maintain an AI-built app by re-prompting?


Yes, for most changes. In Taskade, you ask Taskade EVE for the change in chat, and it edits the app. Re-prompting is the easy half. The other half is verification: test the change with a real record and a second account, check the automation run, and keep the previous revision ready to restore.


How much does vibe coded app maintenance cost?


Most of the cost is time: checking each change, watching for failed steps and reviewing access. Retool's 2026 Build vs. Buy report warns that time saved on one task can be offset by time lost to maintenance. In Taskade, the tool cost is one plan: Free to start, Pro at $10 per month billed annually, and Business at $25 per month billed annually.


How do you verify a change to an AI-built app?


Verify a change against the outcome, not the code. Submit a real form entry, check the record in the project, confirm that the automation ran and that the agent used the new field, then open the app as a second account. Keep the previous revision so you can restore it if the change does not hold.


How does client sign-in work in a Taskade Genesis app?


Client sign-in works on every Taskade plan, including Free. Sign-in confirms who the visitor is. It does not hide other people's records on its own. You match records to the login, for example by an email field, and you test it with a second account before you share the app. Custom domains start on Pro, with up to 10, and are unlimited on Business and up.


Which systems should you not maintain yourself?


Do not maintain systems where a specialist vendor carries the burden: payments, payroll and tax, regulated records and security tools for your staff. Their rules change by country and year, and each adds security debt. Maintain the layer around them that changes every month: the CRM views, client portals, intake forms, dashboards and follow-up steps.

Workspace DNA is the Taskade architecture of Memory, Intelligence and Execution. Projects remember, AI agents reason, and automations run. A Taskade Genesis app serves all three to the people who use it. Each layer writes back into the same workspace, so every change adds to the context the next change starts from.
